title: Modern Stoicism, carefully
hookLine: online Stoicism can drift into toughness and money; the originals aimed at virtue and kindness

lines: A MARBLE BUST AND A COLD SHOWER.
A DIFFERENT SCHOOL IN THEIR CLOTHES?
cards: Scroll for a minute and you'll find it. A marble bust of Marcus Aurelius, lit dramatically, over a caption about cold showers, never showing weakness and crushing your competition.
A video promising Stoic secrets to a seven-figure income. A man in a gym explaining that real Stoics don't cry. Some of it is harmless.
Some of it is useful. But set beside the Stoics you've read this year, some of it sounds like a different school wearing their clothes.

teach.b: First, two spellings. Small-s stoic, in everyday English, means someone who endures without showing feeling. Capital-S Stoic means a member of the school of the painted porch.
The two overlap a little and get confused a lot. Second, the aim.
For Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, the only true good was virtue: wisdom, justice, courage and self-control, lived out with other people.
Money, status, even health were, in their language, indifferent: fine to have, fine to use well, never the point. A Stoic route to riches would have puzzled them.
Seneca was rich, and he spent letters warning himself not to be owned by it. Third, toughness. Endurance mattered to the Stoics, but not coldness.
Epictetus tells his students he shouldn't be unfeeling like a statue; he should keep his relationships as a son, a brother, a citizen.
Marcus reminds himself again and again to be gentle and patient with people who annoy him, and calls kindness hard to defeat when it's real. Fourth, reading the modern stuff.

Not with a sneer: some people find real help in it, and some modern writers handle the sources well. Just with one question. Does this slogan point toward being a better neighbor, more just, more honest, kinder?
Or only toward being harder to hurt and better at winning?

teach.h: CHECK THE SLOGAN AGAINST THE SOURCE.
teach.b: If it's only the second, check the source.

how: Readers of the Stoics often test popular Stoic slogans against the ancient texts, asking whether they point toward virtue and care for others or only toward endurance and success.

o: the Stoic revival, best read with virtue as its aim
a toughness program for hiding every feeling you have
a new school that replaced the old Stoics' ideas

s: for the ancient Stoics, the only true good was virtue
money, status and even health were indifferents.
Epictetus taught his students to have no feelings toward family
he said he shouldn't be unfeeling like a statue, but keep his relationships.
Marcus Aurelius wrote often about being kind to people who annoy him
gentleness and patience run all through the Meditations.

games.q: a video says real Stoics never show weakness and always win. how do you test it?
o: take it on trust because of the marble bust
ask whether it points toward virtue and kindness
dismiss everything modern about the Stoics
games.why: the old Stoics aimed at virtue lived with others; a slogan that's only about winning leaves out the point.

practice: Think of one Stoic-sounding slogan you've heard, maybe control what you can, or don't let them see you sweat, and hold it beside what you've read this year.
Where does it match the old teachers, and where does it leave something out, like kindness, justice or other people? Without judging whoever shared it, notice what's missing, and what you'd add back.

wordCard.voice: Modern Stoicism: the old school's revival today, best read carefully, with the original aim in view, which was virtue and kindness, not toughness and money. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: virtue or excellence, for the Stoics the only true good.

carryVoice: Your line: virtue, not toughness. The old Stoics aimed at kindness, never coldness. Back tomorrow.
